title: Skills and SKILL.md

story: On Monday you spend an afternoon writing down how you like to plan a ticket: when to ask the requester questions first, what a good check looks at, one worked example from the frontend. You save it as ~/.claude/skills/plan-ticket/SKILL.md, open Claude Code and type "plan RH-1234 before we start". Claude writes a plan. It is not bad, but it is Claude's own plan: no questions, no edge case, nothing from your file. Your skill never opened.

Then Dana, a teammate, asks for a copy, so you paste the file into Slack. A week later you improve it, and now there are two versions in the world. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, starts every ticket on a fresh machine, so it has neither of them.
hook.question: What makes Claude open a skill, and how do I ship one copy of it to every person and every agent?

read.h: Claude reads the label, not the book
p: A skill is a folder with one required file, SKILL.md. The file starts with a short block between two --- lines, called the frontmatter, which holds a few YAML fields about the skill. Everything after the second --- is the body: the actual instructions, written for whoever does the task.

The two parts are read at different times, and that is the whole trick. When a session starts, Claude gets a list of every skill it can use, and each entry holds only the skill's name and its description. The bodies stay on disk. When Claude decides that a task matches a description, it calls its Skill tool, and only then does the body enter the conversation. A person can also open a skill on purpose by typing its name as a slash command, such as /plan-ticket. Showing the short part always and the long part only when needed is called progressive disclosure, and it is why you can install fifty skills without filling Claude's memory with fifty manuals.

Now the Monday problem makes sense. Your plan-ticket file had no description field, and when that field is missing Claude Code uses the first non-empty line of the body instead. So the label Claude saw was "# plan-ticket", which says nothing about tickets, questions or checks, and Claude had no reason to open the book. Compare it with the frontmatter of plan-and-grill, the planning skill our platform shares with every engineer:

code.text:
---
name: plan-and-grill
description: "Use before writing code for a ticket or task: decide whether to ask the requester questions first, then write a one-screen plan with the definition of done, 3-5 checks including an edge case, the proof each check needs, an estimate, risks and what is out of scope."
when_to_use: "A Jira ticket, bug report or feature request is about to be built; the user says 'plan this' or 'grill me'; the task is big or vague."
argument-hint: "[Jira key or task description]"
---

notes.text: The name becomes the slash command. In a plugin it gets the plugin's name in front: /rhino-core:plan-and-grill.
What the skill does and when to use it, with the main use case first. Claude decides from this line.
Extra trigger phrases and situations. Claude Code adds them to the description in the skill list.
A hint shown when a person types the slash command, so they know what to put after it.

read.h: Write the description as a trigger
p: Because Claude chooses from the description alone, write it the way you wrote MCP tool descriptions in an earlier lesson: say what the skill produces, then when to use it, in the words a person would really type. "Use before writing code for a ticket" matches "plan RH-1234 before we start"; "Planning notes" matches almost nothing. Put the main use case first, because Claude Code cuts the description and when_to_use together at 1,536 characters in the list.

A description can also be too wide. "Use for any coding task" fires on nearly every request, so its body is loaded into sessions where it does not help. Every description sits in every session, which costs a little context each time, and every body that loads costs more. Claude Code can show you both numbers for a plugin with claude plugin details: the always-on cost of the descriptions and the on-invoke cost of each body.
read.see:
Projected token cost
  Always-on:   ~58 tok   added to every session

Per-component (rounded)
  component     always-on  on-invoke
  welcome-note        ~60        ~70

deeper.h: Go deeper: skills only a person should start
p: Some skills should never start by themselves, such as one that deploys or posts a message to a channel. Add disable-model-invocation: true to the frontmatter and Claude Code leaves the description out of Claude's list completely, so only a person typing the slash command can start the skill. The opposite switch, user-invocable: false, hides the skill from the slash menu, for background knowledge that only Claude should load.

read.h: The body: a goal, reasons, and depth on demand
p: Once a skill loads, its body stays in the conversation for the rest of the session, so keep it short and useful. Start with the goal and the reason for it, then the decisions the reader has to make and the signs that help them decide, then a small example. The docs suggest keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines; ours are much shorter.

Details that only some tasks need go into other files in the same folder, such as references/grill-questions.md. The body says when to read them, so Claude opens them only for the big, vague tickets that need them, and a typo fix never pays for them. How to write this text so that agents follow it well has its own lesson at the end of this part.

code.text:
# plan-and-grill

Goal: agree what "done" means before any code, so the work is checked against the ask, not against itself.

## Ask first, or plan now?
Ask the requester first when the ticket is big, spans teams, or two readings would lead to different code.
Signs: no example, a vague verb ("improve", "support"), a screen with no states, a change to an API others use.
A small, clear fix (a typo, copy, one obvious bug) goes straight to the plan.
For big tasks, read references/grill-questions.md before you ask.

## The plan (one screen)
1. Done means: 1-2 sentences in the user's words.
2. Checks: 3-5, at least one edge case, each with the proof it needs.
3. Estimate, risks, and what is out of scope.

notes.text: The goal, with its reason after the comma.
Signs to look for, so the reader can judge a ticket the skill never saw.
The deeper file loads only for big tasks. Small tasks never pay for it.

read.h: A plugin carries skills to everyone
p: A file in your home folder reaches only you. A plugin is the package that carries skills, and also subagents, hooks and MCP servers, to other machines. It is a folder with a manifest, .claude-plugin/plugin.json, and the skills in a skills/ folder next to it. Only the manifest goes inside .claude-plugin/; everything else sits at the plugin's top level. Every skill gets the plugin's name as a prefix, so welcome-note in the team-notes plugin is called team-notes:welcome-note, and two plugins can never fight over a name.

Plugins are listed in a marketplace, which is a git repository with a catalog file, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json. A person adds the marketplace once and installs plugins from it as name@marketplace, for example team-notes@lab. After that, the plugin's version decides who gets a change. When plugin.json sets a version, everyone stays on that version until you change the string, however many commits you push. So a fixed sentence without a version bump reaches nobody. That is the answer to the two copies in Slack: one plugin, one version, one place to get it.

code.text:
team-notes/                      the plugin folder
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json              the manifest: name, version, description
└── skills/
    ├── welcome-note/
    │   └── SKILL.md             called team-notes:welcome-note
    └── goodbye-note/
        └── SKILL.md

plugin.json:
{
  "name": "team-notes",
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "description": "Short notes for the team: welcomes and goodbyes",
  "author": { "name": "Lab" }
}

notes.text: The only file inside .claude-plugin/ is the manifest.
Skills are namespaced: plugin name, colon, skill name.
The name every skill is namespaced under. Use kebab-case.
Bump it on every change. People stay on a version until it changes.

deeper.h: Go deeper: where else skills live
p: Claude Code also loads skills from your own ~/.claude/skills/ folder (for every project), from a repo's .claude/skills/ folder (for everyone who opens that repo) and from a folder an administrator manages. When two of those have the same name, the administrator's wins over yours, and yours wins over the project's. Plugin skills never collide, because of their prefix.

To try a plugin without installing it, start a session with claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin. It loads for that one session only. Before you publish, run claude plugin validate --strict on the plugin and on the marketplace: it checks the manifests and every SKILL.md frontmatter, and --strict turns warnings, such as a missing version, into failures, which is what a CI job wants.

lab.title: Make Claude notice your skill
needs: A terminal; no model calls until the optional last step
lab.goal: Build a plugin with one skill, list it in a marketplace, and use claude plugin details to see the label Claude reads in every session and the body it reads only on demand.

guess.q: A skill's frontmatter has a name but no description field. What does Claude see about it in its skill list?

options.text: Nothing: a skill without a description is left out of the list.
options.why: It is still listed. Only disable-model-invocation: true takes a skill out of Claude's list.

options.text: The first non-empty line of the body, such as "# plan-ticket".
options.why: When the description is missing, Claude Code falls back to the first line of the body, which is usually a heading that says nothing about when to use the skill.

options.text: The whole body, so Claude can judge it fully.
options.why: Bodies are never in the list. That would put every skill's full text into every session.

follow.say: Make a lab folder and give this terminal its own Claude Code config folder, so nothing in the lab touches your real settings or plugins.
Write a plugin with one skill whose description is as weak as the Monday one, because you will measure the difference later.
follow.do:
mkdir -p plugins/team-notes/.claude-plugin plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note
cat > plugins/team-notes/.claude-plugin/plugin.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "team-notes",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Short notes for the team: welcomes and goodbyes",
  "author": { "name": "Lab" }
}
EOF
cat > plugins/team-notes/skills/welcome-note/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: welcome-note
description: Notes.
---
# welcome-note

Goal: a welcome a new teammate can read in ten seconds, so they feel expected on day one.

Write two lines. The first says hello by first name and names the team. The second gives
one practical tip for the first day, such as where to ask questions. Keep it warm and plain.
EOF
find plugins -type f | sort

follow.say: Validate the plugin, and notice what the validator does not judge: it checks the shape of the files, not whether the description is any good.
Add a marketplace catalog at the top of the lab folder, then add the marketplace and install the plugin from it, the same two steps a teammate would run.
follow.do:
mkdir -p .claude-plugin
cat > .claude-plugin/marketplace.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "lab",
  "description": "Plugins for the academy lab",
  "owner": { "name": "Me" },
  "plugins": [
    { "name": "team-notes", "source": "./plugins/team-notes", "description": "Short notes for the team" }
  ]
}
EOF
claude plugin validate . --strict
claude plugin marketplace add ./
claude plugin install team-notes@lab
follow.see:
✔ Validation passed
Adding marketplace…✔ Successfully added marketplace: lab (declared in user settings)
Installing plugin "team-notes@lab"...✔ Successfully installed plugin: team-notes@lab (scope: user)

lab.build: Add a second skill to the same plugin, plugins/team-notes/skills/goodbye-note/SKILL.md, for a short, warm goodbye when a teammate leaves. Give it a description that says what it writes and a when_to_use line with the phrases people really type ("farewell", "last day"). Bump the version in plugin.json to 0.2.0, run claude plugin validate plugins/team-notes --strict, and check that claude plugin details team-notes@lab now lists two skills. (This lab's marketplace is a folder on your disk, which Claude Code reads in place, so you see changes at once. A marketplace in a git repo, like ours, follows the version.) If you want to see a real session pick the skill (this uses your normal Claude Code plan for one short request), open a new terminal without CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, run claude --plugin-dir ~/academy-labs/p12-1/plugins/team-notes, and ask: "Lior joins the frontend team tomorrow. Can you write something I can post in the team channel?" Watch for the Skill tool loading team-notes:welcome-note.
checks: claude plugin validate plugins/team-notes --strict prints Validation passed.
claude plugin details team-notes@lab shows team-notes 0.2.0 and Skills (2)  goodbye-note, welcome-note.
The always-on number went up when you wrote real descriptions (about 8 tokens with "Notes.", about 113 with two good skills), and you can say why that cost is worth paying.
Each description says what the skill produces and when to use it, in words a person would type.
You can explain why a person who installed 0.1.0 gets your goodbye skill only after the version changes.

solution.text:
---
name: goodbye-note
description: "Writes a short, warm goodbye for a teammate who is leaving: thanks for one real thing they did, and good luck."
when_to_use: "Someone leaves the team, or the user asks for a farewell message or a last-day note."
---
# goodbye-note

Goal: a goodbye the person would be glad to screenshot. Name one real thing they did for the team.

(and in plugin.json: "version": "0.2.0")

explain: Which part of SKILL.md does Claude read in every session, and which part only when it decides to use the skill? Why is it built that way?
Your Monday skill had no description. What label did Claude see, and why did it never open the skill?
You fixed a sentence in a skill and pushed it to the marketplace, but teammates still get the old text. What did you forget, and why does Claude Code work this way?
lab.done: Both validate commands pass, details shows two skills at version 0.2.0, and you found the missing quote in the broken skill.

check.q: A session starts with twenty skills installed. What does Claude know about each skill before it uses any of them?

options.text: The full body of every skill, so it can choose well
options.why: That would put twenty manuals into every session. Bodies load only when a skill is used.

options.text: Each skill's name and description, with when_to_use added
options.why: That short label is all Claude has to decide with, which is why the description is the part to work on.

options.text: Only the names, and it opens each skill to check
options.why: The description is in the list too. Opening every skill to check would defeat the point of loading bodies on demand.

check.q: A plugin's plugin.json says "version": "1.0.0". You fix a wrong command in one of its skills and push to the marketplace. A week later teammates still see the old command. Why?

options.text: Skills are cached for a week before they refresh
options.why: There is no time-based cache. Updates follow the version.

options.text: The marketplace.json must also list each skill's text
options.why: The catalog lists plugins and where to find them, never skill text.

options.text: The version did not change, and a set version keeps everyone on it until the string changes
options.why: Claude Code compares versions to decide whether to update. Same string, no update, however many commits you push.

check.q: A teammate writes a skill with the description "Use for any coding task." What goes wrong?

options.text: It matches almost every request, so its body loads into many sessions where it does not help
options.why: A trigger that matches everything is as unhelpful as one that matches nothing, and each load costs context.

options.text: Claude Code rejects descriptions that start with "Use"
options.why: Starting with "Use when" or "Use before" is actually a good habit; the problem is that this one says no particular situation.

options.text: Nothing; a broad description means the skill is used more, which is good
options.why: Being used is only good when the skill helps the task. A body loaded into unrelated work is noise for the model.

p: Our shared skills live in one private repo, RhinoHealth/claude-plugins, whose catalog is called rhino. It holds four plugins of our own: rhino-core with the skills every engineer gets (plan-and-grill, verify, pr-story and the task skills), and fe-guild, be-guild and devops-guild with each guild's codebase knowledge. Plugins that live in other repos, such as kb for the R&D brain and fcp-lab, are listed by a pinned commit, so a bump is a pull request in this repo. Everyone reads the stable branch; main is a second channel, rhino-latest, for people who want changes first.

fcp's guild skills move out of the repo's agents/ folder into the guild plugins, and fcp's .claude/settings.json registers the rhino marketplace and enables fe-guild and be-guild for contributors who trust the folder. Skills that only make sense inside fcp, such as create-test-data, stay in fcp/.claude/skills. Plugin CI runs claude plugin validate --strict on every manifest, keeps each description plus when_to_use under 600 characters (stricter than Claude Code's 1,536), and fails a pull request that changes a plugin without a higher version.

tickets.why: Creates RhinoHealth/claude-plugins with the rhino catalog, the stable and latest channels, and pinned outside plugins.
Moves fcp's FE and BE skills into the guild plugins and registers the marketplace in fcp's project settings.
plan-and-grill, the first rhino-core skill: a description that fires on the right tasks and a short body.
Plugin CI: validate --strict, frontmatter and description limits, and the version-bump check.

words.plain: A folder with a SKILL.md that teaches one task. Claude loads it when the task matches its description.
The YAML block between two --- lines at the top of SKILL.md: name, description, when_to_use and a few more.
The skill's label: what it does and when to use it. Claude decides from this alone whether to load the skill.
Show the short label in every session, and load the long body only when a task needs it.
A package with .claude-plugin/plugin.json that carries skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers to other machines, with a version.
A git repo with .claude-plugin/marketplace.json that lists plugins people install as name@marketplace.

review.q: Write the frontmatter for a skill that writes release notes from merged PRs. Make it fire on the right requests and on nothing else.
review.a: A name, a description that says what it produces (release notes from merged PRs) and when to use it (before a release, "write the changelog"), and a when_to_use line with real phrases. Nothing so wide that it matches every writing task.

review.q: Explain to a teammate why installing fifty skills does not fill Claude's context with fifty manuals.
review.a: Only each skill's name and description sit in every session; a body loads when Claude picks the skill or a person types its slash command. That is progressive disclosure.

review.q: You changed a skill in a plugin. List what must happen before a teammate's Claude Code uses the new text.
review.a: Bump the version in plugin.json, merge it to the branch the marketplace serves, and the teammate's Claude Code updates (by auto-update or claude plugin update), then a new session loads it.

remember: The description decides whether a skill is opened, the version decides who gets a change, and the marketplace decides where everyone gets it from.
